## Introduction Accurate speech recognition is necessary for human communication and socialization ( Higgins and Semin, 2001) but can be challenging in noisy environments. Normal-hearing listeners presented with speech in noise, however, adapt out of the simultaneous noise and can recognize up to 28% more isolated words or syllables when the speech tokens are presented in continuous noise than when the tokens start at the same time as the noise ( Ainsworth and Meyer, 1994; Cervera and Gonzalez-Alvarez, 2007). Noise adaptation likely occurs because the leading noise adapts the dynamic range of auditory neurons depending on the noise level ( Ainsworth and Meyer, 1994), but the physiological processes underlying noise adaptation remain unclear. Like visual ( Ohzawa et al., 1982) or somatosensory neurons ( Garcia-Lazaro et al., 2007), auditory neurons adapt their response dynamic range to the current environment. For short tones in continuous, steady noise, neurons shift their discharge rate-level functions toward the noise level ( Evans, 1974; Costalupes et al., 1984; Gibson et al., 1985; Phillips and Hall, 1986; Rees and Palmer, 1989). In steady noise, neural dynamic range adaptation (DRA) toward the mean noise level can increase the accuracy with which auditory neurons encode sound intensity, which might improve the encoding of the speech envelope ( Fig. 1 _A_) ( Marrufo-Pérez et al., 2018) and/or the speech spectrum as represented in the auditory nerve ( Fig. 1 _B_) ( Ainsworth and Meyer, 1994). Auditory neurons, however, do not simply adapt their dynamic range to the mean sound level but to the most probable levels in the stimulus ( Dean et al., 2005). Indeed, when the stimulus (noise or tone) level varies every 50 ms according to a statistical distribution of sound levels, and a set of levels is presented 80% of the time (defined as “high probability region”), neurons shift their rate level functions toward the “most commonly occurring sound levels” ( Dean et al., 2005, 2008; Watkins and Barbour, 2008, 2011; Wen et al., 2009, 2012). When the stimulus level is distributed in two high-probability regions, neurons do not adapt to the mean level (which lays between the two regions). Instead, some neurons shift their dynamic range toward one level region and other neurons shift it toward the other region ( Dean et al., 2005). These adjustments improve the coding precision of levels near the high probability region in the neural population ( Dean et al., 2005; Wen et al., 2009; but see Rocchi and Ramachandran, 2018). Most auditory neurons adapt with a time course of 100-400 ms ( Dean et al., 2008; Wen et al., 2012), and DRA has been observed in the auditory nerve ( Wen et al., 2009, 2012), the inferior colliculus ( Dean et al., 2005, 2008; Robinson et al., 2016; Bakay et al., 2018), and the auditory cortex ( Watkins and Barbour, 2008, 2011) of animals, as well as in the human auditory cortex ( Herrmann et al., 2018, 2019). The aim of the present study was to investigate how noise adaptation in human speech recognition depends on the noise level distribution. We compared adaptation for noise-masked words preceded by adapting noise precursors with different noise level distributions, going from steady, to mildly fluctuating to highly fluctuating. Neural DRA was expected to be less for the highly fluctuating precursor because it does not provide a “most common” level to which neurons can adapt their dynamic ranges. We also investigated the effects of fast-amplitude compression on noise adaptation. Fast-amplitude compression could facilitate adaptation by turning a highly fluctuating sound into a lessfluctuating one, thus allowing auditory neurons to adapt to a prevailing level. Fast compression occurs at multiple auditory processing stages, is often reduced in impaired hearing, and is applied by many hearing devices (see Bacon et al., 2004). If it facilitates adaptation, this might shed light on why speech-in-noise recognition is more challenging for hearing-impaired than for normal-hearing listeners, even in aided conditions (e.g., Glasberg and Moore, 1989; Johannesen et al., 2016).

Our eyes need tears to stay healthy and comfortable. If your eyes do not produce enough tears, it is called dry eye. Dry eye is also when your eyes do not make the right type of tears or when your tears dry out too quickly. In this article: - How do tears work? - Dry eye video - Dry eye symptoms - Dry eye causes - Dry eye diagnosis - Dry eye treatment - Dry eye prevention tips ### Video: How to Say Bye to Dry Eye !Video: How to Say Bye to Dry Eye► ## How Do Tears Work? When you blink, tears spread over the eye. This keeps the eye’s surface smooth and clear. Tears are important for good vision. Tears are made of three layers: - An oily layer - A watery layer - A mucus layer Each layer of your tears serves a purpose. The **oily layer** is the outside of the tears. It makes the tear surface smooth and keeps tears from drying up too quickly. This layer comes from the meibomian glands in the eyelids. The **watery layer** is the middle of the tears. It makes up most of what we see as tears. This layer cleans the eye, washing away particles that do not belong in the eye. This layer comes from the lacrimal glands in the eyelids. The **mucus layer** is the inner layer of the tears. This helps spread the watery layer over the eye’s surface, keeping it moist. Without mucus, tears would not stick to the eye. Mucus is made in the conjunctiva. This is the clear tissue that covers the white of your eye and inside your eyelids. Normally, our eyes constantly make tears to stay moist. If our eyes are irritated, or we cry, our eyes make a lot of tears. But, sometimes the eyes don’t make enough tears or something affects one or more layers of the tears. In those cases, we end up with dry eyes. _Back to the top of the article._ ### Video: Dry Eye Symptoms, Causes and Treatments !Video: Dry Eye Symptoms, Causes and Treatments► ## What Does Dry Eye Feel Like? Here are some of the symptoms of dry eye. - You feel like your eyes are stinging and burning. - Blurred vision, especially when reading - There is a scratchy or gritty feeling like something is in your eye. - There are strings of mucus in or around your eyes. - Your eyes are red or irritated. This is especially true when you are in the wind or near cigarette smoke. - It is painful to wear contact lenses. - You have lots of tears in your eyes. Having a lot of tears in your eyes with dry eye might sound odd. But your eyes make more tears when they are irritated by dry eye. _Back to the top of the article._ ## What Are the Main Causes of Dry Eye? People tend to make fewer tears as they get older due to hormonal changes. Both men and women can get dry eye. However, it is more common in women—especially those who have gone through menopause. Here are some other causes of dry eye. - Certain diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren’s syndrome, thyroid disease, and lupus - Blepharitis (when eyelids are swollen or red) - Entropion (when eyelids turn in); ectropion (eyelids turn outward) - Being in smoke, wind or a very dry climate - Looking at a computer screen for a long time, reading and other activities that reduce blinking - Using contact lenses for a long time - Having refractive eye surgery, such as LASIK - Taking certain medicines, such as: - Diuretics (water pills) for high blood pressure - Beta-blockers, for heart problems or high blood pressure - Allergy and cold medicines (antihistamines) - Sleeping pills - Anxiety and antidepressant medicines - Heartburn medicines Tell your ophthalmologist about all the prescription and non-prescription medicines you take.

**Thermal Sensation and Peripheral Thermoreceptor Function in Hands and Feet During Winter Sports**  

---

**Abstract**  
Thermal perception in human extremities plays a critical role in maintaining comfort, safety, and performance during outdoor activities in cold environments. This paper examines the physiological mechanisms underlying temperature sensation in the skin of the hands and feet, with emphasis on the role of peripheral thermoreceptors. Drawing upon neurophysiological research and field observations in winter sport contexts, we analyze how varying ambient temperatures and mechanical factors influence thermoreceptor activity, signal transduction, and subjective temperature perception. The findings underscore the importance of localized sensory responses in extremities, their contribution to thermoregulation, and implications for protective equipment design.

---

**1. Introduction**  
The human somatosensory system is equipped with specialized receptors that detect changes in thermal stimuli. These thermoreceptors—classified broadly as cold and warm receptors—are distributed throughout the skin and are particularly significant in the distal extremities, such as the hands and feet [1]. During winter sports, these body parts are frequently exposed to rapid temperature fluctuations and mechanical stress, rendering them vulnerable to cold-related performance decrements and injury. Understanding the mechanisms of thermal sensation in these regions is essential for optimizing athlete safety and comfort in low-temperature environments.

---

**2. Peripheral Thermoreceptor Physiology**  
Thermoreceptors in the skin are free nerve endings located within the dermis and epidermis. Cold-sensitive receptors are primarily associated with Aδ fibers, which conduct signals rapidly, and warm-sensitive receptors are linked to C fibers, which conduct more slowly [2]. The density of cold receptors in the hands and feet is higher than in proximal body regions, reflecting the need for fine-tuned sensory feedback in extremities that interact directly with the environment.

Activation of cold receptors occurs when the local skin temperature drops below a threshold, often around 30–32 °C, with increased firing rates as temperatures decline further [3]. Warm receptors, in contrast, are activated by increases above baseline skin temperature. Both receptor types exhibit dynamic and static responses: dynamic responses signal rapid changes, while static responses indicate sustained thermal states.

---

**3. Thermal Sensation During Winter Sports**  
Winter sports such as skiing, snowboarding, and ice climbing expose the hands and feet to ambient temperatures well below freezing, often compounded by wind chill and contact with cold surfaces. Gloves and boots provide insulation, yet factors such as moisture accumulation, compression of insulating materials, and restricted blood flow can compromise their effectiveness [4].  

Peripheral thermoreceptors continuously monitor skin temperature and relay information to the central nervous system, where integration with other sensory inputs produces the subjective perception of cold or warmth. In cold environments, vasoconstriction in extremities reduces warm blood flow, lowering skin temperature and increasing cold receptor activity [5]. This heightened receptor firing rate contributes to the sharp sensation of cold often reported by athletes in exposed conditions.

---

**4. Modulation of Thermal Perception**  
Thermal perception is not solely determined by ambient temperature; mechanical pressure, moisture, and adaptive receptor responses also play significant roles. Prolonged exposure to cold can lead to receptor adaptation, wherein firing rates decrease despite continued low temperatures, potentially dulling sensation and increasing risk of frostbite [6]. Conversely, rapid temperature changes—such as removing gloves in sub-zero air—can produce exaggerated sensations due to the dynamic responsiveness of thermoreceptors.

The extremities’ thermosensory function is further influenced by central modulation. For instance, during intense physical activity, metabolic heat production may alter core temperature, which in turn affects peripheral blood flow and receptor sensitivity [7]. Athletes may perceive less cold in the hands during periods of high exertion, even if skin temperatures remain low.

---

**5. Implications for Equipment Design and Safety**  
Knowledge of thermoreceptor function has direct applications in developing protective gear for winter sports. Materials that minimize rapid skin temperature changes can reduce dynamic cold receptor activation, thereby improving comfort. Layering strategies that manage moisture and prevent conductive heat loss help maintain skin temperatures within a range that avoids excessive receptor stimulation.  

In addition, understanding the thresholds and adaptation behaviors of thermoreceptors can inform training protocols, ensuring athletes recognize early signs of potentially dangerous cold exposure before sensory dulling occurs.

---

**6. Conclusion**  
Thermal sensation in the hands and feet during winter sports is governed by the complex interplay of peripheral thermoreceptor activity, environmental conditions, and physiological regulation. Cold and warm receptors provide critical sensory feedback that influences both performance and safety. By integrating neurophysiological insights with practical considerations for equipment and environmental management, winter sport participants can better protect extremities from harmful cold exposure while maintaining optimal sensory function.

**Report: Industrial Dissolution of Sucrose in Fermentation Systems for Ethanol Production**  

---

**Abstract**  
The dissolution of sucrose in aqueous media is a critical preparatory stage in large-scale ethanol fermentation. This report examines the operational procedures employed in industrial fermentation facilities to ensure efficient sucrose solubilization, focusing on mechanical agitation systems, temperature regulation, and solubility control. The discussion integrates engineering considerations with physicochemical principles to highlight how controlled dissolution impacts downstream fermentation performance.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
In ethanol production from sugar-based feedstocks, sucrose must be dissolved into a fermentable solution prior to inoculation with microbial cultures. The dissolution step directly influences substrate availability, fermentation kinetics, and product yield. Industrial operations typically handle thousands of liters of solution, requiring specialized equipment and process design to achieve uniform solubilization without localized concentration gradients that could inhibit microbial activity.  

---

**2. Mechanical Agitation in Large Fermentation Tanks**  
Mechanical agitation is the primary driver for sucrose dissolution at scale. Fermentation tanks are equipped with impellers—often of the axial flow or radial flow type—mounted on vertical shafts. The choice of impeller geometry is determined by the viscosity of the medium and the required mixing intensity.  

- **Axial flow impellers** (e.g., pitched-blade turbines) promote bulk circulation, moving liquid vertically within the tank to minimize stratification.  
- **Radial flow impellers** (e.g., flat-blade turbines) generate high shear forces, which aid in breaking down crystalline aggregates and dispersing sucrose particles evenly through the solvent.  

Mixing speed is optimized to balance dissolution rate and energy consumption; excessive agitation can lead to foaming or mechanical stress on tank components.  

---

**3. Temperature Regulation and Solubility Control**  
Sucrose solubility in water is temperature-dependent, increasing markedly with rising temperature. Industrial systems employ heat exchangers or steam jackets to bring the solvent to an optimal temperature range (commonly 50–60 °C) before sucrose addition. This temperature window ensures rapid dissolution while avoiding thermal degradation of sucrose or caramelization.  

Temperature sensors integrated into the control system maintain setpoints within ±1 °C, and automated dosing systems meter sucrose into the tank at a controlled rate to prevent supersaturation and crystallization.  

---

**4. Process Monitoring and Quality Assurance**  
Continuous monitoring of solution concentration is achieved through inline refractometers or density meters. These instruments provide real-time feedback on the degree of dissolution, enabling operators to adjust agitation speed, temperature, or feed rate dynamically.  

Sampling ports allow for periodic laboratory verification of sugar concentration, pH, and microbial compatibility. Ensuring complete dissolution prior to fermentation inoculation helps prevent osmotic stress on yeast or bacterial cultures, which can hinder ethanol yields.  

---

**5. Scale-Up Considerations**  
When scaling from pilot-scale fermenters to full industrial tanks, hydrodynamic parameters such as Reynolds number and power number are carefully evaluated. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling may be employed to predict mixing patterns and identify potential dead zones where sucrose dissolution could be incomplete.  

Large tanks often feature baffles to disrupt vortex formation, enhancing mixing efficiency. In some configurations, dual-impeller systems are installed at different heights to address vertical gradients in concentration and temperature.  

---

**6. Integration with Downstream Fermentation**  
Once sucrose is fully dissolved and the solution cooled to fermentation temperature (typically 30–35 °C for yeast-based ethanol production), the liquid is transferred or maintained in the same vessel for inoculation. The dissolution process must be synchronized with fermentation scheduling to minimize holding time, reducing the risk of microbial contamination.  

---

**7. Conclusion**  
Efficient sucrose dissolution in industrial fermentation tanks is achieved through the integration of mechanical agitation, precise temperature regulation, and continuous monitoring. Optimizing these parameters ensures that sucrose is fully available for microbial metabolism, supporting high ethanol yields and consistent process performance. The engineering strategies described here form the foundation of reliable, large-scale ethanol production from sucrose-rich feedstocks.

### Limited support or contradictive observations for trichromacy advantage Superior color discrimination abilities of trichromacy are demonstrated in behavioral experiments for captive New World monkeys (Caine et al. 2003; Pessoa et al. 2005; Saito et al. 2005a; Smith et al. 2003b). Finding fruits amid tropical foliage has long been proffered as an adaptive explanation for primate trichromacy. Nevertheless, field observations of free-ranging animals have provided only limited support for simple trichromacy advantage. In a mixed-species troop of saddleback ( _Saguinus fuscicollis_) and mustached ( _S. mystax_) tamarins, trichromats are further from their neighbors during vigilance than their dichromatic conspecifics. This is explained as resulting from the potentially better perception of predation risk in trichromats (Smith et al. 2005). In a population of white-faced capuchin monkeys ( _C. capucinus_), dichromats sniff more figs and take longer foraging sequences than trichromats, especially for cryptic figs, and the trichromat phenotype with the most spectrally separated L/M opsin alleles shows the highest acceptance index for conspicuous figs (Melin et al. 2009). However, there are no differences in feeding rates among phenotypes (Melin et al. 2009). Results of other behavioral observations of wild New World monkeys have produced equivocal results or results contradictory to the predictions from the trichromat advantage hypothesis. In the wild mixed-species troops of tamarins, the color vision types (dichromatic or trichromatic) do not show a consistent effect on the leadership of the troops to feeding trees (Smith et al. 2003a). In other social groups of tamarins ( _S. imperator imperator_ and _S. fuscicollis weddelli_) no significant difference is detected between females (thought to consist of trichromats and dichromats) and males (all dichromats) in their ability to locate or discriminate between feeding sites (Dominy et al. 2003a). In a population of capuchin monkeys ( _C. capucinus_), no significant difference is detected between trichromats and dichromats in feeding or energy intake rates (Vogel et al. 2007). In another population of the same capuchin monkey species, no difference is detected between dichromats and trichromats in time spent foraging on different food types (Melin et al. 2008). In a free-ranging social group of black-handed spider monkeys, dichromats are not inferior to trichromats in frequency, accuracy, and unit-time intake efficiency of detecting fruits (Hiramatsu et al. 2008). This is explained because the luminance contrast of fruits to background leaves is the main determinant of fruit detection in both dichromats and trichromats on the basis of colorimetric measurement of fruits and background leaves (Hiramatsu et al. 2008). In this social group of spider monkeys, irrespective of color vision phenotypes, the monkeys sniff and reject visually cryptic fruits more often than visually conspicuous fruits, implying that color vision is not the sole determinant for ingestion or rejection of fruits (Hiramatsu et al. 2009). ### Dichromat advantage Even dichromat advantage is reported in foraging for camouflaged insects in wild capuchins (Melin et al. 2007, 2010) and in wild and captive tamarins (Smith et al. 2012) and in foraging under low light intensity in captive marmosets (Caine et al. 2010). In fact, dichromats are reported to superior to trichromats at breaking camouflage caused by variegated backgrounds (Morgan et al. 1992; Saito et al. 2005b). These findings of observational studies in natural environments suggest that the superior ability of trichromats to see the red–green color contrast may not translate into a selective advantage. ### Direct evaluation of fitness effect of trichromacy Fedigan et al. 2014 tested whether color vision phenotype is a significant predictor of female fitness in a population of wild capuchins, using 26 years of long-term survival and fertility data. No advantage to trichromats over dichromats for three fitness measures (fertility rates, offspring survival and maternal survival) was found. This finding suggests that a selective mechanism other than simple trichromat advantage (heterozygote advantage) is operating to maintain the color vision polymorphism. More attention should be directed to testing in field studies the alternative mechanisms of balancing selection proposed to explain opsin polymorphism: niche-divergence, frequency-dependence and mutual benefit of association (Fedigan et al. 2014).

**The Art and Evolution of Foley: Crafting Environmental Sounds for the Silver Screen**  

In the world of motion pictures, the magic of storytelling extends far beyond what unfolds visually on screen. While audiences may be captivated by sweeping vistas, intricate set designs, and nuanced performances, the sonic landscape plays an equally vital role in creating an immersive cinematic experience. Among the most indispensable tools in a sound designer’s arsenal are *foley effects*—the carefully crafted environmental noises that breathe life into scenes, from the crunch of footsteps on gravel to the groan of an ancient door.  

### A Brief History of Foley  

The term “foley” owes its origin to Jack Foley, a pioneering sound artist who, in the early days of synchronized sound films, recognized the need for realistic, synchronized audio effects to complement on-screen action. Before his innovations, many films relied on generic sound libraries, resulting in mismatched or flat auditory experiences. Foley’s approach was revolutionary: he performed sounds live, in sync with the film’s projection, using an array of props and surfaces to replicate everyday noises. This practice quickly became a standard in the industry, with dedicated foley stages built to accommodate the variety of sounds needed for different productions.  

By the mid-20th century, foley had established itself as a distinct discipline within sound design. Studios employed specialized artists who, often working in pairs, would watch scenes repeatedly while experimenting with objects—boots, fabric, wood, metal, and even food—to achieve the perfect auditory illusion. The tactile, performance-based nature of foley distinguished it from other sound production methods, embedding it deeply in cinematic tradition.  

### Techniques for Simulating Environmental Sounds  

Creating convincing environmental sounds requires both technical skill and creative problem-solving. At its core, foley is about matching the *emotion* and *texture* of a sound to the visual narrative, not merely replicating the real-world source.  

- **Footsteps:** Perhaps the most common foley task, footsteps vary widely depending on the surface, footwear, and character’s gait. Foley artists maintain collections of shoes and floor panels—wood, concrete, metal grates, dirt—to ensure authenticity. A soldier’s heavy boots on cobblestone demand a different timbre than a child’s sneakers on a tiled kitchen floor.  
   
- **Doors and Hinges:** The creak of a door can communicate tension, age, or neglect. In practice, foley teams often use old wardrobe hinges, manipulated slowly, to produce the long, resonant groan associated with horror or suspense scenes. Conversely, a brisk, well-oiled hinge might signal a modern, well-maintained setting.  

- **Fabric Movement:** Subtle rustling of clothing can indicate mood or movement. Heavy coats produce a muffled, thick sound, while silk generates a whisper-like swish. These effects are often recorded in close proximity to the microphone to capture fine detail.  

- **Impact and Object Handling:** Whether it’s the clink of glassware or the thud of a dropped book, these sounds must be timed precisely to align with the actors’ actions. Foley stages are often filled with miscellaneous props, allowing artists to improvise based on the scene’s demands.  

### Controversies and Debates in Foley Practice  

While foley is widely celebrated for its artistry, it’s not without its controversies. One ongoing debate centers around the balance between realism and dramatic enhancement. Purists argue that environmental sounds should faithfully replicate real-world acoustics, maintaining authenticity. Others contend that sound design is inherently interpretive; exaggerating certain effects can heighten emotional impact.  

An example lies in the portrayal of footsteps in high-intensity scenes. Real footsteps may be subtle, especially on soft surfaces, but amplifying them—and adding a sharper transient—can emphasize urgency or menace. Critics of this practice suggest it risks breaking immersion if the sound seems implausible. Proponents counter that audiences subconsciously accept heightened soundscapes as part of cinematic language.  

Another point of contention is the increasing use of digital sound libraries in place of live foley recording. Technological advances allow sound editors to access vast archives of pre-recorded effects, often at lower cost and faster turnaround. This has led to concerns about the decline of traditional foley artistry, as well as the uniformity of sound across productions that rely heavily on the same library sources. Supporters of digital methods note that they can be combined with live recording, offering flexibility and efficiency without sacrificing creativity.  

### The Enduring Role of Foley in Modern Cinema  

Despite these debates, foley remains integral to the auditory fabric of film. Its tactile, human-driven approach ensures that environmental sounds feel rooted in the scene’s physical reality. Even in an era of advanced digital audio manipulation, many directors and sound supervisors insist on live foley sessions for critical sequences, citing the subtle imperfections and organic variations they produce.  

Moreover, foley is not simply about sound replication—it’s about storytelling. The muffled thump of footsteps in a dimly lit hallway can build suspense; the cheerful squeak of a door in a sunny kitchen can signal comfort and familiarity. These effects shape the audience’s emotional journey as much as dialogue or musical score.  

### Conclusion  

From its origins in the early sound era to its place in high-budget contemporary productions, foley has continually adapted to the evolving needs of filmmakers. It bridges the gap between the visual and auditory realms, ensuring that every creak, rustle, and footstep resonates with purpose. While technological trends may shift the methods used to create these effects, the artistry and narrative power of foley endure—reminding us that in cinema, the smallest sounds can have the greatest impact.  

In the end, the legacy of foley is not just in the noises it produces, but in the way it enriches the worlds we see on screen, making them feel as tangible and lived-in as the reality outside the theater doors.

**Aerodynamic Implications of Asymmetrical Vent Placement in Wind Tunnel Models**  

---

**Abstract**  
The aerodynamic performance of structures is highly sensitive to the placement and geometry of ventilation openings. This paper presents an analysis of asymmetrical vent placements in scale wind tunnel models, examining their impact on airflow distribution, turbulence generation, and drag coefficients across different sections of a test structure. Using controlled experiments in a closed-circuit wind tunnel, the study quantifies changes in pressure differentials, vortex shedding patterns, and boundary layer behavior resulting from non-uniform vent arrangements. Results indicate that asymmetry in vent configuration produces localized turbulence zones and modifies global flow patterns, with measurable consequences for net aerodynamic efficiency.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Ventilation openings serve dual purposes in architectural and vehicular structures: facilitating internal air exchange and influencing external aerodynamic behavior. While symmetrical vent placement has traditionally been favored for its predictable flow characteristics, asymmetrical configurations are often necessitated by functional constraints, design aesthetics, or structural limitations. Understanding the aerodynamic consequences of such asymmetry is critical for optimizing performance in contexts ranging from high-speed transport vehicles to large-scale buildings.

Previous research has predominantly addressed symmetrical vent arrays, documenting reductions in drag and improvements in cooling efficiency under uniform conditions [1,2]. However, limited attention has been given to the aerodynamic complexities introduced when vents are offset or irregularly spaced. This study aims to address that gap by systematically analyzing airflow patterns through asymmetrically vented models under controlled wind tunnel conditions.

---

**2. Methodology**  

**2.1 Wind Tunnel Setup**  
Experiments were conducted in a closed-loop wind tunnel with a test section measuring 1.5 m by 1.5 m, capable of generating free-stream velocities from 5 m/s to 50 m/s. The tunnel was equipped with a multi-point pitot-static measurement system and Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) for flow visualization.

**2.2 Model Design**  
Two sets of scale models were fabricated from rigid polymer composite: one with symmetrical vent placement (control group) and another with varying degrees of asymmetry in vent location and size. Vent cross-sections were kept constant at 0.02 m², while the spacing from the model’s central axis varied between 0.05 m and 0.15 m.

**2.3 Measurement Parameters**  
Key aerodynamic parameters measured included:  
- Drag coefficient (Cd) via force balance instrumentation  
- Pressure distribution across the surface using flush-mounted transducers  
- Turbulence intensity derived from PIV data  
- Vortex shedding frequency identified from spectral analysis of wake velocity fluctuations

---

**3. Results**  

**3.1 Pressure Distribution**  
Asymmetrical vent placement produced marked pressure differentials between the leeward and windward sides of the model. Maximum pressure drop across a vent occurred when it was positioned closer to the leading edge on one side, resulting in localized acceleration of airflow within the vent opening and increased suction on the opposite surface.

**3.2 Turbulence and Wake Structure**  
PIV imagery revealed that asymmetry introduced a skew in the wake structure, shifting the primary vortex street laterally. Turbulence intensity downstream of the asymmetrically vented side was up to 18% higher than in the symmetrical control. This skewed wake led to uneven loading forces across the structure, potentially impacting mechanical stability in full-scale applications.

**3.3 Drag Coefficient Variation**  
Drag coefficients for asymmetrical configurations were consistently higher, with increases ranging from 4% to 11% depending on vent offset magnitude. The increase was attributed to both enhanced form drag from disturbed boundary layers and induced drag from asymmetric wake behavior.

---

**4. Discussion**  
The data indicate that vent asymmetry significantly alters both localized and global aerodynamic characteristics. The lateral displacement of vents disrupts the uniformity of the boundary layer, causing premature separation on one side and extended attachment on the other. This imbalance not only elevates drag but also modifies cross-flow patterns within and around the structure.

From a design perspective, certain asymmetrical configurations may be advantageous if targeted airflow redirection is desired—for example, channeling external flow toward specific cooling zones. However, such benefits must be weighed against the increased turbulence and drag penalties observed. In high-speed applications, even minor asymmetry can result in performance losses that outweigh functional gains.

Moreover, the altered vortex shedding behavior has implications for structural vibration. Uneven shedding frequencies can introduce asymmetric oscillatory forces, potentially leading to resonance conditions in susceptible designs. This suggests a need for integrated aerodynamic-structural analysis when implementing non-uniform vent placements.

---

**5. Conclusion**  
Asymmetrical vent placement exerts a measurable influence on aerodynamic efficiency, primarily by increasing turbulence intensity and elevating drag coefficients. While functional constraints may necessitate such configurations, designers should account for the resultant flow alterations and their potential impact on stability and energy performance. Future research should explore computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling of asymmetrical vent scenarios to complement experimental findings and facilitate predictive optimization.

---

**References**  
[1] Smith, J., & Lee, R. (2018). Ventilation array optimization for aerodynamic performance. *Journal of Wind Engineering*, 146, 23–34.  
[2] Gomez, L., & Hartman, P. (2019). Symmetry effects on drag reduction in ventilated structures. *Applied Fluid Mechanics Review*, 12(4), 201–215.  
[3] Tanaka, M., & Zhou, Q. (2021). Wake dynamics in asymmetrical bluff bodies. *International Journal of Fluid Dynamics*, 55(2), 89–104.

With respect to this aspect, our study is methodologically different from the paw preference counts used in other work (e.g., in cats, McDowell et al., 2018; summarised in Wells, 2020). However, we see no reason to believe that the owners provided incorrect information, or that this could have led to a bias in a specific direction (e.g., toward the right paw). Many studies have focused on handedness as proxy for lateralization, highlighting that population-level biases in handedness seem to be characteristic of most animals, although the strength and direction varies between species. Gender has been found to influence handedness in some species; in humans, for instance, males are more likely to be left-handed than females. Another aspect that has been comparatively unexplored is the role of age in shaping functional asymmetries, especially in adulthood. Handedness has been widely explored in dogs ( _Canis familiaris_), although there are contrasting findings about the influence of the dogs’ sex and age, possibly due to the comparatively small sample sizes used in previous studies. Here we overcame this issue by investigating these effects in a unique sample of 17,901 dogs of unknown neutered status. Specifically, this study used pre-collected data from the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC)’s ‘Test Your Pet’ survey, during which owners tested their dogs’ paw preference in retrieving food from a tube in 3 consecutive trials. Based on the results of these 3 trials, owners were asked to assess whether their dogs used their left or right forepaw most of the time, or if it was difficult to tell. 13,240 dogs were scored as having a paw preference (i.e., were not ambidextrous or ambiguous), representing 74.0 % of the dogs tested. In those dogs that showed a paw preference, there was a population-level right-paw preference in both male and female dogs (60.7 % female and 56.1 % male), however, the proportion of dogs with a right-paw preference was significantly higher in females than males. Elderly dogs also tended to show a stronger right-paw preference than younger dogs. We conclude that the effect of sex on handedness may be influenced by factors such as sex hormones, while age changes may reflect the development of handedness and its maintenance in dog populations.

**Artificial Lighting and the Disruption of Nocturnal Sleep Cycles in Domestic Animals: Physiological Implications for Dogs and Other Pets**  

---

**Abstract**  
Artificial lighting in urban and domestic environments has become a pervasive element of modern life, yet its impact on the circadian and sleep regulation of nocturnal and crepuscular animals remains incompletely understood. This paper examines the physiological effects of chronic exposure to artificial light—specifically urban streetlights and indoor illumination—on the sleep cycles of domestic dogs and other companion animals. Drawing on recent chronobiology research, we explore the mechanisms by which photic stimuli influence melatonin secretion, retinal adaptation, and behavioral rhythms, and we discuss implications for animal welfare in urbanized settings.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
The proliferation of artificial light sources in both outdoor and indoor environments has dramatically altered natural photoperiods for many species. While humans have adapted to extended light exposure with relatively predictable circadian shifts, domestic animals—particularly those with nocturnal or crepuscular tendencies—may experience more pronounced disruptions in their sleep cycles. Dogs (Canis familiaris), though often diurnal in human households, retain physiological features inherited from ancestral canids that are adapted to low-light conditions [1]. The widespread use of high-intensity LED streetlights and indoor illumination has introduced novel light spectra into their living environments, potentially influencing their sleep quality and timing.  

---

**2. Nocturnal and Crepuscular Physiology in Domestic Dogs**  
Domestic dogs display a flexible activity pattern that can shift toward nocturnal or crepuscular behavior depending on environmental cues and household routines [2]. Their visual system includes a high proportion of rod photoreceptors, enabling effective low-light vision, and a reflective tapetum lucidum layer that enhances light capture. This adaptation, while beneficial for visual acuity in dim environments, also increases sensitivity to artificial light sources at night. Exposure to prolonged illumination may reduce the amplitude of natural melatonin cycles, a hormone closely associated with sleep regulation [3].  

---

**3. Artificial Light Sources and Spectral Composition**  
Streetlights in urban areas have transitioned from sodium-vapor lamps to broad-spectrum LEDs, which emit higher proportions of short-wavelength (blue) light. This spectrum has been shown to exert stronger effects on circadian photoreception in mammals, mediated by intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) [4]. Indoor lighting, particularly compact fluorescents and LEDs, similarly introduces blue-rich wavelengths into nighttime environments. For dogs and other pets, these wavelengths may cause phase delays in circadian rhythms, leading to shifts in sleep onset and wake times.  

---

**4. Physiological Effects of Chronic Light Exposure**  
Chronic exposure to artificial light during natural rest periods can result in several physiological changes:  
- **Melatonin Suppression:** Blue-rich light suppresses pineal melatonin production, leading to reduced sleep propensity and altered REM sleep patterns [5].  
- **Retinal Overstimulation:** In species with a tapetum lucidum, nocturnal exposure to bright artificial light may cause prolonged afterimages or photic stress, potentially influencing comfort and behavior.  
- **Thermoregulatory Impacts:** Circadian disruption can affect core body temperature cycles, indirectly influencing sleep architecture.  

---

**5. Behavioral Consequences**  
Owners may observe changes in pets’ nighttime behavior, such as increased restlessness, delayed sleep onset, or heightened alertness in response to outdoor stimuli. Dogs exposed to constant urban lighting may also exhibit reduced periods of deep sleep, impacting recovery and overall health. Similar patterns have been documented in other domestic animals, including cats and small mammals, which may attempt to seek darker environments when possible [6].  

---

**6. Mitigation Strategies**  
Several approaches can reduce the impact of artificial lighting on animal sleep cycles:  
- **Environmental Control:** Use of blackout curtains or dimmed indoor lighting during evening hours.  
- **Light Spectrum Adjustment:** Preference for warm-spectrum bulbs with lower blue light content to minimize circadian disruption.  
- **Adaptive Scheduling:** Aligning feeding and activity patterns with natural light-dark cycles to reinforce physiological rhythms.  

---

**7. Conclusion**  
Artificial lighting is an often-overlooked environmental factor influencing the sleep cycles of domestic animals. Dogs and other pets, particularly those with visual adaptations for low-light vision, are susceptible to circadian disruption through chronic exposure to urban streetlights and indoor illumination. Understanding the physiological pathways affected by light exposure can inform better environmental management in urban households, ultimately supporting animal welfare and health.  

---

**References**

[2] Rehn, T., & Keeling, L. J. (2016). *Activity Patterns in Domestic Dogs*. Applied Animal Behaviour Science, 174, 76–84.  
[3] Kennaway, D. J., & Wright, H. (2002). *Melatonin and Circadian Rhythms in Animals*. Comparative Biochemistry and Physiology, 132(3), 505–513.

**Abstract**  
The phenomenon of directional dominance in plants, expressed through consistent patterns of growth and movement, is a subject of considerable interest in plant physiology and evolutionary biology. This paper examines limb-like dominance in plants through the lens of phototropism and thigmotropism, emphasizing the genetic and environmental determinants of twining direction around supports. Particular attention is given to the molecular mechanisms underlying these tropic responses, the evolutionary advantages conferred by consistent directional growth, and the variability observed across taxa. The synthesis of recent empirical findings suggests that twining directionality is not randomly distributed but rather reflects an interplay between inherited traits and local environmental stimuli.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Directional growth behaviors in plants are widely recognized as adaptive strategies facilitating resource acquisition and structural stability. While plants lack limbs in the animal sense, their organs—stems, tendrils, and petioles—can exhibit dominance in movement or orientation, akin to lateralized behaviors in other organisms. Two primary tropic responses, phototropism and thigmotropism, govern much of this directional behavior. Phototropism refers to growth in response to light stimuli, typically mediated by differential cell elongation on opposing sides of an organ [Darwin & Darwin, 1880]. Thigmotropism denotes growth in response to touch or mechanical stimulation, often resulting in coiling or twining around a support [Jaffe & Galston, 1968]. The consistent directionality of twining—clockwise or counterclockwise—has been documented in numerous species and is hypothesized to arise from both genetic predisposition and environmental modulation.

---

**2. Phototropism and Directional Bias**  
Phototropism is driven primarily by the redistribution of auxin, a plant hormone that promotes cell elongation. In shoots, exposure to unilateral light causes auxin to accumulate on the shaded side, resulting in curvature toward the light source [Briggs, 1963]. This curvature itself may exhibit a directional bias depending on the plant’s morphological asymmetries or the arrangement of its vascular tissues. For example, certain species display a consistent rotation of the shoot apex during phototropic bending, which can influence subsequent thigmotropic interactions with nearby supports. Genetic studies have identified phototropin proteins (phototropin 1 and phototropin 2) as key mediators of light perception and directional growth [Christie et al., 1999]. In some cases, allelic variation in these proteins correlates with subtle differences in growth orientation, suggesting that directional bias in phototropism may have a heritable component.

---

**3. Thigmotropism and Twining Directionality**  
Thigmotropism involves the perception of mechanical stimuli via mechanosensitive ion channels in the plant cell membrane. Upon contact with a support, tendrils or stems initiate a coiling response, often in a specific direction. This twining direction—clockwise (dextrorotatory) or counterclockwise (sinistrorotatory)—is remarkably consistent within species. For instance, *Humulus lupulus* (common hop) twines clockwise, whereas *Phaseolus vulgaris* (common bean) twines counterclockwise [Gorham, 1881]. The underlying cause of this directional preference has been linked to asymmetries in cortical microtubule orientation and the arrangement of cellulose microfibrils during cell wall deposition [Furutani et al., 2000]. These cellular features are genetically encoded, and thus twining direction can be considered a morphological trait subject to evolutionary selection.

---

**4. Genetic and Environmental Interactions**  
While genetic determinants set the baseline for directional growth tendencies, environmental factors can modulate or override these tendencies. Light direction, wind patterns, and the spatial arrangement of supports can influence the initiation and maintenance of twining behavior. Experimental reversal of light gradients has been shown to alter the initial direction of phototropic bending, though the subsequent thigmotropic coiling often reverts to the genetically programmed direction [Silk & Erickson, 1979]. Moreover, mechanical stress from wind or contact with multiple supports can induce atypical twining patterns, though these are generally transient.

---

**5. Evolutionary Considerations**  
The evolutionary significance of consistent twining directionality may lie in the efficiency of climbing and the avoidance of self-entanglement. Uniform coiling direction across individuals of a species may facilitate predictable structural arrangements in dense vegetation, reducing mechanical interference among neighboring plants. Directional dominance in phototropism could similarly optimize light capture by orienting leaves and stems in a manner that minimizes shading of conspecifics. Comparative studies across phylogenetically diverse climbers suggest that directional twining has arisen multiple times, indicating convergent evolution toward stable mechanical strategies [Isnard & Silk, 2009].

---

**6. Conclusion**  
Directional dominance in plant growth, whether expressed through phototropic bending or thigmotropic coiling, represents a complex interplay between genetic programming and environmental modulation. The consistent twining direction observed in many species underscores the role of heritable traits in shaping plant behavior. Future research integrating molecular genetics, biomechanics, and ecological modeling will deepen our understanding of how and why plants exhibit such directional preferences, with potential applications in agriculture, horticulture, and biomimetic design.

---

**Tropical Palm Fruits in Decorative Craft: Structural Patterns and Aesthetic Applications**  

Tropical palm fruits have long been valued not only for their nutritional and economic importance but also for their distinctive structural features that lend themselves to ornamental use. Among these features, surface patterns resembling holes, dimples, or depressions have been prominent in the crafting traditions of various cultures. These markings, which are naturally occurring in certain species, have influenced both the functional and aesthetic dimensions of palm fruit carving.  

---

### 1. Botanical Context  

Palm fruits, produced by members of the family Arecaceae, display a wide range of morphologies depending on species, maturity stage, and environmental conditions. The hard endocarp, or shell, in many tropical species serves as a durable substrate for artistic modification. In particular, fruits such as *Cocos nucifera*, *Borassus flabellifer*, and *Attalea speciosa* possess distinctive external features—ranging from fibrous husks to rigid shells—that offer natural points of interest for artisans [1].  

The outer surface of the endocarp may include patterned indentations or pores that arise during fruit development. These can be symmetrically arranged, often in a small set of repeated forms, and are sometimes mistaken for damage or wear. In reality, they are integral to the fruit’s anatomy, marking areas of internal connection between the seed and its surrounding tissue.  

---

### 2. Cultural Significance in Craft Traditions  

In many coastal and island societies, palm fruits serve as a readily available medium for decorative arts. The naturally occurring dimples or “holes” are often incorporated into the design rather than removed or altered. Carvers may use these patterns as focal points, framing them with incised motifs or integrating them into symbolic imagery.  

For example, in Pacific island carving traditions, artisans sometimes orient the fruit so that the natural depressions form the “face” of a mask or figurine. In Southeast Asia, certain ceremonial vessels fashioned from palm fruit shells feature the indentations prominently, aligning them with geometric engravings or inlaid materials. The unmodified patterns are seen as enhancing authenticity, conveying a sense of organic origin even after extensive shaping.  

---

### 3. Structural Influence on Carving Techniques  

The presence of natural indentations affects the technical approach to working with palm fruits. The depressions often mark areas of thinner shell material, which can influence how and where a carver chooses to cut or bore. In some species, these points provide convenient starting locations for creating openings, as less force is required to penetrate the shell.  

Artisans aware of the internal structure will typically plan their designs to avoid compromising the fruit’s integrity. The orientation of the depressions relative to the grain of the shell material can determine the stability of carved pieces. This is particularly important when producing functional objects such as ladles, containers, or musical instruments, where durability is essential.  

---

### 4. Decorative Aesthetics and Symbolism  

Beyond their practical implications, the dimple-like features of palm fruits have been imbued with symbolic meaning in various traditions. In some craft cultures, the repeated patterns are interpreted as representations of eyes or celestial bodies, lending a spiritual dimension to the finished object.  

The tripartite arrangement found in certain fruits is especially noteworthy from an aesthetic standpoint. Artists may highlight this arrangement through contrasting materials, pigments, or incised borders. When polished, the natural indentations catch light differently than the surrounding shell, creating subtle visual emphasis. Such effects are prized in decorative pieces intended for display in communal or ceremonial settings.  

---

### 5. Modern Adaptations  

Contemporary artisans and designers have continued to explore the decorative potential of palm fruit surface patterns. In modern craft markets, carved palm shells often retain their natural indentations as an indicator of authenticity and craftsmanship. The patterns are sometimes enhanced with resin filling, metallic inlays, or colored lacquers to create striking visual contrasts.  

In addition to traditional hand-carving, machine-assisted techniques such as CNC engraving and laser etching now allow for precise integration of natural patterns into complex designs. This has expanded the scope of palm fruit craft, enabling larger-scale production while preserving the organic features valued by collectors and cultural practitioners alike.  

---

### 6. Preservation and Sustainable Use  

The use of palm fruits in decorative crafts raises considerations regarding sustainability and resource management. Harvesting practices that respect the ecological role of the fruit—both as a food source and as part of the reproductive cycle—are vital. Some communities employ selective gathering methods, taking only mature or naturally fallen fruits for craft purposes.  

Preservation of traditional carving knowledge is equally important. The understanding of how natural surface patterns can be incorporated into design is often passed down through apprenticeship and oral instruction. Documenting these techniques ensures that future generations can continue to benefit from the aesthetic and functional potential of tropical palm fruits.  

---

### Conclusion  

The structural features of tropical palm fruits, including naturally occurring dimples and hole-like patterns, have played a significant role in shaping decorative craft traditions across diverse cultures. These patterns influence both the technical execution and the visual appeal of carved objects, serving as points of inspiration for artisans past and present. By respecting the organic origins of these features and adapting them to modern techniques, craft practitioners maintain a link between botanical form and artistic expression, ensuring the continued relevance of palm fruits in decorative arts.

The **visual field** is "that portion of space in which objects are visible at the same moment during steady fixation of the gaze in one direction";[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-Traquair-1) in ophthalmology and neurology the emphasis is mostly on the structure inside the visual field and it is then considered “the field of functional capacity obtained and recorded by means of perimetry”.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-Strasburger_Poeppel-4) However, the visual field can also be understood as a predominantly _perceptual_ concept and its definition then becomes that of the "spatial array of visual sensations available to observation in introspectionist psychological experiments"[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-5) (for example in van Doorn et al., 2013).[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-6) The corresponding concept for optical instruments and image sensors is the field of view (FOV). In humans and animals, the FOV refers to the area visible when eye movements – if possible for the species – are allowed. In optometry, ophthalmology, and neurology, a visual field test is used to determine whether the visual field is affected by diseases that cause local scotoma or a more extensive loss of vision or a reduction in sensitivity (increase in threshold). ## Normal limits \ [edit\] [](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Traquair_1938_Fig_1_modified.png) The classical image on the shape and size of the visual field by Harry Moss Traquair in his book _Clinical Perimetry_ (1938; modified to show the essentials). It shows that the visual field is considerably larger on the temporal side than the often quoted 90° extent. Similar limits were already reported in the 19th century. The normal (monocular) human visual field extends to approximately 60 degrees nasally (toward the nose, or inward) from the vertical meridian in each eye, to 107 degrees temporally (away from the nose, or outwards) from the vertical meridian, and approximately 70 degrees above and 80 below the horizontal meridian.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-R%C3%B6nne-7)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-Traquair-1)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-9) The binocular visual field is the superimposition of the two monocular fields. In the binocular field, the area left of the vertical meridian is referred to as the left visual field (which is located temporally for the left, and nasally for the right eye); a corresponding definition holds for the right visual field. The four areas delimited by the vertical and horizontal meridian are referred to as upper/lower left/right quadrants. In the European Union, the minimum field requirement for driving is 50 degrees to either side of the vertical meridian and 120 degrees horizontally in total, and 20 degrees above and below the horizontal meridian. The macula corresponds to the central 17 degrees diameter of the visual field; the fovea to the central 5.2 degrees, and the foveola to 1–1.2 degrees diameter.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-Strasburger-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-erratum-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-Polyak-12) Note that in the clinical literature the fovea can refer to the central 1–1.2 deg, i.e. what is otherwise known as the foveola, and can be referred to as the "clinical fovea".[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_field?utm_source=chatgpt.com#cite_note-myths-13) The nose is situated in the field of view of both eyes, but due to later processing carried out in the brain, it is not noticed during normal visual tasks. ## Measuring the visual field \ [edit\] Main article: Visual field test The visual field is measured by perimetry. This may be kinetic, where spots of light are shown on the white interior of a half sphere and slowly moved inwards until the observer sees them, or static, where the light spots are flashed at varying intensities at fixed locations in the sphere until detected by the subject. Commonly used perimeters are the automated Humphrey Field Analyzer, Optopol Perimeters, Octopus, the Heidelberg Edge Perimeter, the Oculus or the Olleyes VisuALL. Another method is to use a campimeter, a small device with a flat screen designed to measure the central visual field. Light spot patterns testing the central 24 degrees or 30 degrees of the visual field, are most commonly used. Most perimeters are also capable of testing up to 80 or 90 or even 120 degrees. Another method is for the practitioner to hold up one, two, or five fingers in the four quadrants and center of a patient's visual field (with the other eye covered). This is also known as confrontational field testing. If the patient is able to report the number of fingers properly as compared with the visual field of the practitioner, the normal result is recorded as "full to finger counting" (often abbreviated FTFC). The blind spot can also be assessed via holding a small object between the practitioner and the patient. By comparing when the object disappears for the practitioner, a subject's blind spot can be identified. There are many variants of this type of exam (e.g., wiggling fingers in the visual periphery on the cardinal axes).

**Sensory Processing Alterations Following Intensive Meditation Retreats: Comparative Thresholds for External Stimuli**  

---

**Abstract**  
Prolonged meditation practice has been associated with changes in attentional control, emotional regulation, and sensory perception. This study examines alterations in sensory thresholds for external stimuli in experienced meditators before and after attending intensive residential retreats lasting between 10 and 30 days. Using controlled auditory and tactile stimulation paradigms, we evaluated the minimal stimulus intensity required to elicit conscious detection and measured reaction times to supra-threshold stimuli. Results indicate that post-retreat participants exhibit elevated sensory thresholds alongside faster discrimination accuracy for salient stimuli, suggesting a selective gating mechanism enhanced through sustained meditative practice. These findings contribute to the growing evidence that meditation can modulate sensory processing, potentially through neuroplastic changes in thalamo-cortical networks.

---

**Introduction**  
Meditation, particularly in its concentrated and prolonged forms, has been shown to influence cognitive and perceptual systems [1,2]. Intensive retreats, often involving several hours of daily practice in silence, provide a unique context in which sensory processing can be examined under sustained attentional training and reduced environmental complexity. While prior research has focused on the attentional and emotional benefits of meditation [3], relatively fewer studies have investigated changes in sensory detection thresholds as a function of prolonged practice.  

The present study seeks to address this gap by investigating whether experienced meditators demonstrate measurable changes in their capacity to detect and respond to external stimuli after completing an intensive retreat. We hypothesize that meditation-induced modulation of sensory gating may influence both the sensitivity to low-intensity stimuli and the efficiency of processing high-salience signals.

---

**Methods**  
**Participants**  
Twenty-four experienced meditators (mean practice duration: 8.3 ± 2.1 years) were recruited from retreat centers. All participants completed a residential retreat lasting between 10 and 30 days, adhering to daily schedules of 8–12 hours of formal meditation practice.  

**Stimuli and Procedure**  
Auditory stimuli consisted of pure tones at varying decibel levels (20–50 dB SPL), while tactile stimuli were delivered via vibrotactile actuators positioned on the index finger (amplitude range: 0.05–0.5 mm displacement). Pre-retreat and post-retreat sessions were conducted in a sound-attenuated chamber under standardized lighting. Participants were instructed to indicate stimulus detection via button press. Reaction times and detection rates were recorded.  

**Data Analysis**  
Sensory threshold was defined as the lowest stimulus intensity yielding ≥ 50% detection rate over 20 trials. Repeated measures ANOVA compared pre- and post-retreat thresholds and reaction times for both modalities.

---

**Results**  
Participants demonstrated a statistically significant increase in sensory thresholds post-retreat for both auditory (mean increase: 4.6 dB; *p* < 0.01) and tactile stimuli (mean increase: 0.08 mm displacement; *p* < 0.05). Despite elevated thresholds, reaction times to supra-threshold stimuli decreased significantly post-retreat (auditory: mean decrease 37 ms; tactile: mean decrease 29 ms; *p* < 0.05).  

These results suggest that meditators became less responsive to low-intensity, non-salient stimuli, yet maintained or improved their responsiveness to stimuli exceeding a certain intensity. Participants reported a subjective sense of “quieter” perception during daily life following the retreat, consistent with quantitative findings.

---

**Discussion**  
The elevation of sensory thresholds following intensive meditation may reflect enhanced top-down modulation of sensory input, potentially mediated by changes in thalamic gating and cortical attentional networks [4,5]. By sustaining focused attention on internal states and minimizing engagement with external distractions, meditators may recalibrate the balance between sensory receptivity and cognitive control.  

The concurrent improvement in reaction times to salient stimuli suggests that this recalibration does not impair the ability to respond to important environmental cues. Instead, it may optimize perceptual systems to prioritize relevant signals while filtering out low-priority inputs, consistent with the attentional control models proposed in contemplative neuroscience [6].  

Further research using neuroimaging could elucidate the neural correlates of these changes, particularly in relation to thalamo-cortical connectivity and sensory cortex excitability. Longitudinal designs might also determine whether these threshold shifts persist beyond the immediate post-retreat period.

---

**Conclusion**  
Intensive meditation retreats appear to induce a dual effect on sensory processing: raising detection thresholds for low-intensity stimuli while enhancing responsiveness to salient signals. These findings highlight the capacity of sustained contemplative practice to reshape perceptual systems, with implications for understanding the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying meditation-related sensory modulation.

---

## Overview The NIOSH recommended exposure limit (REL) for occupational noise exposure is 85 A-weighted decibels (dBA) over an eight-hour shift. If workers are repeatedly exposed to noise at or above the REL, employers must provide a hearing loss prevention program. Noise levels are likely hazardous if a person must raise their voice to speak with someone is an arm's length away. Hearing loss from routine noise exposure is 100% preventable and is best addressed by creating a quieter workplace. ### Did you know?‎ Decibels (dB) are a scale for measuring noise. A-weighted noise levels or dBA is used to predict hearing risk. Noise above 85 dBA is considered hazardous. ## Measure noise exposure To properly control and reduce noise in the workplace, you should know: - how loud an area is - how much noise reaches a worker's ear - the frequency content of the noise - where the noise is coming from Occupational noise measurements are usually reported in the following ways: - Sound level is the noise level measurement at a given point in time. - Time Weighted Average (TWA) is sound level averaged over an eight-hour period. - Noise dose is the percent of allowable noise exposure a worker can have. A noise dose of 100% or more means that a worker has exceeded their daily limit for noise exposure. The two basic instruments for characterizing noise are sound level meters (SLMs) and dosimeters. You can use SLMs to: - assess area noise - discover how much noise is coming from specific equipment - get a general idea of frequency content When noise levels in an area are fairly constant, you can use SLMs to estimate the noise exposure in an area. Use personal noise dosimeters to best assess a worker's personal noise exposure. Dosimeters average noise levels over time and calculate a noise dose. ### Did you know?‎ Time Weighted Average (TWA) is the average noise level during a shift (usually 8 hours). It considers both noise levels and how long the employee is exposed at each noise level. ## Create and use a noise map Measure workplace areas with a sound level meter (SLM) and create a noise map of facility areas. If an SLM is not available, sound measurement apps can provide a measure of area noise but may not comply with regulatory requirements. **The Enduring Allure of Blue: Cultural Symbolism and Historical Significance**  

From the deep lapis lazuli in ancient tombs to the indigo-dyed textiles of distant trade routes, the color blue has held a distinct and often exalted place in human culture. Unlike colors readily found in nature—such as earthy browns or leafy greens—blue was historically rare and costly to produce, a fact that imbued it with layers of meaning across civilizations.  

**Ancient Origins and Sacred Associations**  
In ancient Egypt, blue pigments were laboriously created from minerals such as azurite and lapis lazuli, imported from remote mines in what is now Afghanistan. Egyptian artisans used blue to decorate jewelry, ceramics, and the walls of sacred spaces. The hue was associated with the heavens, the Nile, and divine protection, symbolizing life and rebirth. Blue faience amulets were worn to invoke the gods’ favor, and tomb paintings often depicted deities with blue hair or skin to mark their otherworldly nature.  

**Blue in Religious Iconography**  
Across cultures, blue has been linked to spirituality and transcendence. In Christian art of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, the Virgin Mary was frequently depicted wearing robes of deep ultramarine—a pigment derived from lapis lazuli and more valuable than gold. This choice was not merely aesthetic; it signified purity, humility, and the celestial realm. Similarly, in Hindu tradition, gods such as Krishna and Vishnu are often portrayed with blue skin, symbolizing their infinite nature and cosmic scope.  

**The Economics of Rarity**  
The scarcity of blue pigments shaped its cultural perception. Indigo, sourced from plants in India, Africa, and later the Americas, became a prized commodity in global trade. Its rich, stable dye transformed textiles into luxury goods, and its economic significance rivaled that of spices and precious metals. The difficulty of obtaining blue meant that its use was often reserved for royalty, religious leaders, and ceremonial contexts, reinforcing its association with prestige and authority.  

**Blue in Architecture and Design**  
Beyond textiles and art, blue found its way into architecture. In Islamic art and architecture, intricate blue tilework adorns mosques from Samarkand to Istanbul, symbolizing both the infinite nature of the divine and the clarity of the sky. In East Asia, cobalt blue porcelain became a hallmark of Chinese craftsmanship, influencing ceramic traditions worldwide. In Europe, blue stained glass in cathedrals filtered sunlight into a serene, contemplative glow, enhancing the spiritual atmosphere.  

**Shifts in Modern Perception**  
The Industrial Revolution democratized blue. Synthetic dyes allowed mass production of blue clothing, from workmen’s denim to military uniforms, shifting its meaning from elite exclusivity to practicality and reliability. In the 20th century, blue became a staple in corporate branding, chosen for its associations with trust, stability, and professionalism. At the same time, artists such as Picasso explored the emotional depth of blue, using it to convey melancholy and introspection in his famed “Blue Period.”  

**Blue in Contemporary Culture**  
Today, blue remains one of the most popular colors worldwide. It is the color of countless national flags, sports teams, and technological interfaces. Digital screens emit a characteristic blue light, linking the color to modern life and innovation. Yet, even in this ubiquity, blue retains its historical echoes—its ties to the sky and sea, its aura of calmness, and its legacy as a color once reserved for the sacred and the rare.  

**Conclusion**  
The story of blue is one of transformation: from a pigment mined in distant mountains and traded across continents, to a color woven into the fabric of everyday life. Its journey through human history reflects changing technologies, economies, and values, but its symbolism—spanning divinity, prestige, and tranquility—remains remarkably resilient. Blue’s enduring appeal lies not only in its visual beauty but in the centuries of meaning layered into its depths, making it as culturally rich as it is aesthetically striking.

**Silk Production in Domesticated Silkworms**  

Silk, one of the oldest and most prized natural fibers, is produced primarily by the domesticated silkworm *Bombyx mori*. Its cultivation and processing have played a pivotal role in the development of textile industries across diverse cultures for millennia. This entry examines the biology of the silkworm, the methods of sericulture, the harvesting of cocoons, and the economic significance of silk in contemporary global markets.  

---

**Biology of the Domesticated Silkworm**  

The domesticated silkworm is a lepidopteran insect whose larval stage produces silk as a protective casing during metamorphosis. *Bombyx mori* has been selectively bred over centuries to maximize silk yield, resulting in strains that produce larger, denser cocoons than their wild counterparts. The life cycle begins with the hatching of eggs into larvae, which feed voraciously on mulberry leaves. After several molts, the mature larva spins a continuous filament of fibroin protein coated with sericin, forming a cocoon around itself. The filament length can reach 800–1,200 meters, an attribute critical to commercial silk production.  

---

**Sericulture Practices**  

Sericulture—the cultivation of silkworms for silk—requires controlled environmental conditions. Farmers maintain optimal temperature (around 23–28°C) and humidity (65–75%) to ensure healthy larval growth. Mulberry cultivation is an integral component, as leaves must be supplied fresh and free from contaminants.  

Larvae are raised in trays or on shelves, with regular cleaning to prevent disease. At maturity, they are transferred to spinning frames where they construct their cocoons over 2–3 days. Timing is crucial: cocoons intended for silk harvest are collected before the emerging moth can break the filament, which would shorten fibers and reduce quality.  

---

**Cocoon Harvesting and Processing**  

Once spinning is complete, cocoons are gathered and subjected to stifling—exposure to heat or steam—to terminate the pupa and preserve filament integrity. This step also softens the sericin coating, facilitating reeling.  

Reeling involves unwinding the continuous silk filament from the cocoon. Several filaments are combined to form a raw silk thread of desired thickness. The raw silk is then degummed to remove residual sericin, yielding lustrous fibroin strands ready for dyeing and weaving. By-products, such as broken cocoons and pupal residue, are utilized in other industries, including animal feed and cosmetics.  

---

**Economic Importance**  

Silk production has historically been a cornerstone of trade, exemplified by the Silk Road networks that connected East and West. Today, China and India dominate global silk output, with smaller contributions from countries such as Thailand, Uzbekistan, and Brazil.  

The textile industry values silk for its unique combination of strength, sheen, and drape. It is used in high-end fashion, upholstery, and traditional garments. Additionally, silk fibroin has found applications in biomedical fields, including sutures, tissue engineering scaffolds, and drug delivery systems.  

Market fluctuations in silk prices are influenced by labor costs, mulberry crop yields, and competition from synthetic fibers. Nevertheless, demand for natural silk remains robust in luxury segments. Efforts to improve sustainability in sericulture—through organic mulberry farming, waste minimization, and ethical cocoon processing—are shaping modern industry practices.  

---

**Conclusion**  

The production of silk from domesticated silkworms is a complex, labor-intensive process that integrates agricultural skill, biological understanding, and textile craftsmanship. From the cultivation of mulberry trees to the meticulous reeling of filaments, each stage contributes to the creation of a fiber that continues to hold cultural and economic significance worldwide. The enduring appeal of silk, coupled with advancements in sericulture technology, ensures its ongoing role in both traditional and innovative applications in the global marketplace.
